children: The 2026 U.S. midterm elections will determine control of Congress, the direction of both parties and the future of President Trump's agenda. They will also offer early clues about the political forces that may define 2028.
At The Wall Street Journal, our focus this election is simple: helping you understand the people, places and ideas shaping the country.

Our coverage is built around three questions. Who are the power brokers and hopefuls that most embody this moment in American politics? Which communities and conversations reveal what is shaping voters' lives and the decisions they'll make at the ballot box? And what are the cultural discussions that foreshadow where the country is heading?

That approach will take readers beyond Washington and into the places where politics is lived. Our Rooted In series takes our reporters back to their hometowns, bringing context and firsthand reporting to the economic, cultural and political dynamics at work. You'll see chief political correspondent Josh Dawsey returning to his alma mater, the University of South Carolina, while politics reporter Sabrina Rodriguez is taking us to her childhood home in Miami. Others will fan out across the country. And through a body of deeply reported profiles, we examine the candidates who will shape the direction of their parties and the country.

We will also deploy technology to power our storytelling. We've created an AI tool that has ingested the digital world-think millions of TikToks and thousands of hours of podcasts-to help us track and understand what conversations are animating the electorate. We'll analyze the shifts that could decide this election and tell you what they mean. This is not a poll and it is not a replacement for reporting. It is one way to identify emerging themes, contextualize what we are seeing and explain the evidence behind our work.

The formats will vary-written stories, video, graphics, newsletters, live discussions and election-night tools-but the standard will not. Our journalists will choose the questions, verify the material and make the editorial judgments. Our responsibility is to be objective, factual, balanced and clear about what we know, what we are learning and what remains uncertain.
At its core, our approach is to start with the reader, deliver distinctive journalism and make sure every visit to the Journal gives you a clearer view of the world.

We hope you will follow the coverage, give us your feedback and tell us what you need to understand this consequential election. As always, we thank you for the trust you put in us. We will continue to earn it every day.
Sincerely,  Emma Tucker Editor in Chief, The Wall Street Journal
